@graph.headline: What Is JOMO? The Joy of Missing Out, Explained (and How to Practice It)
@graph.description: JOMO means the joy of missing out. Learn where the term came from, how it differs from FOMO and digital detox, and 7 simple ways to practice it.

acceptedAnswer.text: JOMO means “joy of missing out”: the contentment of skipping something on purpose and being glad you did. Merriam-Webster classes it as informal and dates its first known use to 2012.

Anil Dash is most often credited, thanks to his July 19, 2012 blog post “JOMO!” Merriam-Webster names no originator and Word Spy lists an earlier February 2012 tweet, so “popularized by Dash” is the safest wording.

mainEntity.name: JOMO vs FOMO: what is the difference?

acceptedAnswer.text: FOMO is anxiety that others are having rewarding experiences without you. JOMO is contentment with what you chose to skip. FOMO pushes toward constant connection; JOMO asks what you actually want to spend time on.

No, not when it is working. JOMO means choosing which plans deserve your time, often so you can show up better for the ones that matter. It becomes a problem when it turns into avoidance or isolation.

Decide your priorities first, learn one short and kind way to decline, silence nonessential notifications, set a boundary around feeds, and protect one unplanned evening a week. The seven ways above give the full plan.

mainEntity.name: JOMO vs digital detox vs minimalism: which is which?

acceptedAnswer.text: JOMO is a mindset about enjoying what you leave out. A digital detox is a time-limited break from devices or platforms. Minimalism is a broader approach to owning and doing less. They work well together, but none requires the others.

Yes: use response windows instead of instant replies, skip optional meetings that do not need you, and mute low-value channels. Check expectations with your manager, especially in roles that need availability.
